concepts.title: Why Do We Need a Constitution?

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Why Do We Need a Constitution?' refers to.
questions.a: A constitution performs three jobs at once: it supplies the basic rules for how government is constituted and run, it lays down limits on what rulers may do to citizens, and it expresses the aspirations and identity of the people. Every association from a club to a country needs agreed rules; a nation's rules must also bind the powerful.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Why Do We Need a Constitution?'.
questions.a: A constitution is the rulebook for government, the fence around power, and the self-portrait of a people.

concepts.title: The Authority of a Constitution: Constituent Assembly and Legitimacy

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'The Authority of a Constitution: Constituent Assembly and Legitimacy' refers to.
questions.a: A constitution commands obedience only if people accept its authority. That acceptance comes from two sources: the manner of its making -- drafted by an authorised constituent body and ratified by the people -- and its substantive wisdom. India's Constitution drew both from the Constituent Assembly, elected indirectly under the 1946 Cabinet Mission plan, which worked for nearly three years through open debate.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'The Authority of a Constitution: Constituent Assembly and Legitimacy'.
questions.a: Made by the people's representatives, argued openly, accepted by habit and performance -- that is constitutional legitimacy.

questions.q: Under which section is 'The Authority of a Constitution: Constituent Assembly and Legitimacy' taught, and from which source text?

concepts.title: Preamble: The Identity Card of the Constitution

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Preamble: The Identity Card of the Constitution' refers to.
questions.a: The Preamble announces the Constitution's aims: India as a sovereign, socialist, secular, democratic republic securing justice, liberty, equality and fraternity. It is the Constitution's identity card -- summarising the values against which every provision can be read and judged.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Preamble: The Identity Card of the Constitution'.
questions.a: Read the whole book through its first page -- the Preamble fixes the values the machinery must serve.

questions.q: Under which section is 'Preamble: The Identity Card of the Constitution' taught, and from which source text?
questions.a: 1.3 (source: keps201.txt lines 240-330 (the preamble, sovereign socialist secular democratic republic, justice liberty equality fraternity, objectives resolution))

concepts.title: Procedural and Substantive Achievements of a Constitution

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Procedural and Substantive Achievements of a Constitution' refers to.
questions.a: A constitution succeeds in two ways. Procedurally, it must create effective, accountable government -- clear rules of representation, division of power and amendment. Substantively, it must actually restrain power and advance the people's welfare; a constitution that fails one part fails overall, as India's must be judged on both counts.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Procedural and Substantive Achievements of a Constitution'.
questions.a: Good machinery plus real restraint plus delivered justice -- constitutions must work, not merely read well.
